content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) in 1975 as a collaborative initiative with the cruise vessel industry. The primary objective of the VSP is to assist the cruise industry in developing and implementing comprehensive sanitation programs to safeguard the health of passengers and crew aboard cruise vessels. Cruise vessels with foreign itineraries, carrying 13 or more passengers, and calling on a U.S. port are subject to biannual operational inspections and, if necessary, re-inspections by the VSP. Vessel owners are required to pay a fee for these inspections, which is determined based on the gross registered tonnage (GRT) of the vessel. The VSP Operations Manual, available on the VSP website, provides detailed information about these inspections. Additionally, cruise vessel owners or shipyards constructing or renovating cruise vessels may voluntarily request plan reviews, on-site shipyard construction inspections, and/or final construction inspections before the vessel's first or next operational inspection. Fees for on-site and final construction inspections are also based on the vessel's GRT, but no fees are charged for plan reviews or consultations. Section 3.0 of the manual outlines the procedures for requesting plan reviews and construction-related inspections. The guidelines, previously known as the Recommended Shipbuilding Construction Guidelines for Cruise Vessels Destined to Call on U.S. Ports, are now referred to as the Vessel Sanitation Program Construction Manual. These guidelines aim to provide consistent construction and design standards to protect the health of passengers and crew. The CDC reviewed numerous references from various sources to develop these guidelines, which cover aspects of public health on vessels, including food storage, preparation, and service; water bunkering, storage, disinfection, and distribution. Vessel owners and operators can choose designs and equipment that meet their needs, provided they comply with sanitary design criteria established by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) or equivalent organizations, as well as VSP's operational inspection requirements. The guidelines are not intended to restrict the introduction of new designs, materials, or technologies in shipbuilding. Shipbuilders, owners, manufacturers, or other interested parties may request periodic reviews or revisions of the guidelines to incorporate new information or technology. VSP evaluates such requests based on criteria outlined in Section 2.0, Revisions and Recommended Changes. New cruise vessels must comply with all international code requirements, including those of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Conventions, such as the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) Convention, the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), and others. These guidelines, effective June 1, 2005, apply to vessels that lay keel or undergo major renovations after this date. Minor renovations, such as the installation or removal of single pieces of equipment, are not subject to these guidelines. VSP conducts routine vessel sanitation inspections and re-inspections in accordance with the VSP Operations Manual. Periodic reviews and revisions of the guidelines are conducted in collaboration with industry representatives and other stakeholders to keep pace with industry innovations. Recommendations for changes or additions to the guidelines must be submitted in writing to the VSP Chief, including the section to be revised, the proposed change, the rationale, and supporting research or test results. To request plan reviews, consultations, or construction-related inspections, vessel owners or shipyards must submit a formal written request to the VSP Chief as early as possible in the planning, construction, or renovation process. Requests requiring foreign travel must be submitted at least 60 days before the intended visit. VSP assigns primary and secondary officers to coordinate with vessel representatives throughout the process. Plan reviews for new construction typically occur 18-24 months before the vessel's delivery and take two working days to complete. These reviews are conducted in Atlanta, Georgia; Fort Lauderdale, Florida; or other agreed-upon locations. Representatives from the shipyard, vessel owner, and subcontractors should attend the review with all relevant plans, drawings, and equipment specifications. On-site construction inspections are usually conducted in shipyards outside the United States and require a formal written request to the VSP Chief 60 days before the inspection date. These inspections typically involve one to three officers, depending on the vessel's size and design class, and take approximately five working days, including travel. A written report is provided to the requesting party, and the shipyard must submit a corrective action statement addressing any identified issues before the vessel's arrival in the United States. Final construction inspections may be requested by vessel owners or shipyards and are scheduled as soon as possible after the vessel's completion or at least 10 days before its arrival in the United States. If a final construction inspection is not requested, VSP will conduct an unannounced operational inspection within four weeks of the vessel's arrival. VSP schedules operational inspections in accordance with the VSP Operations Manual. The guidelines also establish standards for equipment and materials installed on cruise vessels. While VSP does not test, certify, or endorse specific equipment, it recognizes certifications from independent testing laboratories such as NSF International, Underwriter's Laboratories (UL), and ANSI. Equipment not meeting recommended standards is reviewed by a committee comprising VSP, the cruise ship industry, and independent testing organizations. These definitions cover various aspects of vessel sanitation, including water systems, food contact surfaces, and waste management systems.
